utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution, assisted by my case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends, everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for General Rasim Delic. Our case manager is Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the witness please be sworn in. Make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis, I believe this is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. I believe last week, the Trial Chamber granted an oral decision granting the witness protective measures in the form of facial distortion and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown the document PT06241, which is the pseudonym sheet for the witness, please, and I would ask that we do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just so that you're aware, during the course of this cross-examination I will be confronting this witness with the statements of one or two other witnesses, and when I do so, I will obviously follow the guidelines that the Trial Chamber issued in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. My name is Nicholas Robson, and I'll be asking you questions today on behalf of General Rasim Delic. If at any time you don't understand your questions -- my questions, please, could you let me know, and I'll either repeat the question or try and clarify the question. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, your statement, given to the Office of the Prosecution, has been admitted into evidence. In making that statement, you were interviewed on two different occasions. On the first occasion, you were interviewed on the 10th of March, 2000, and then the second occasion was one year later on the 8th of March, 2001. According to your statement, you met with two different investigators. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why there was such a big gap between the interviews when you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Those weren't different investigators. They were different interpreters, though. When I -- they weren't different investigators. They were different interpreters. The statements that were taken and the investigation that was conducted at the police station in Banja Luka, same investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. But the question was: Was there any reason why the interview stopped in the year 2000 and you had to wait nearly one whole year before you met again with the investigator to complete your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I can assume. During the investigation, I was promised that I would not have to testify. That was as far as the investigator was able to make any promises of that kind. And then maybe the next year there was more information that was needed, maybe some refining the statement. I don't really understand much about the process, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could it be that the reason the interview was halted in the year 2000 was because you couldn't remember much about the events in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I still can't. I probably couldn't back then, not every single detail. It wasn't possible to remember every single little thing. The circumstances back then were not normal. That was more like a chimera mirror. You felt you were half asleep but still stuck in the middle of a nightmare. It was difficult to remember details. You may at one time or another skip a thing or two, just forget about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, when you were interviewed in the year 2000, you would agree with me that that was approximately five years after the events that took place in Vozuca?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've told us that it wasn't possible to remember everything, every single detail. Would you accept that when you gave your interview in the year 2000 and the year 2001, your recollection of events were not so clear?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Some were, some weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is this the first time that you've ever testified before a court about the events in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we can consider what you've said in your statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, you explained that in September 1995, you were a member of the VRS and you were deployed to the Ozren region near to Vozuca. You then explain how, on the 10th of September, 1995, the ARBiH launched an attack and that you and several other members of the VRS tried to pull back and escape; is that so?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You then go on to explain how you met up with other VRS soldiers and how you all wandered around the region during the following days. You explained that after six or seven days, your group decided that if you came across any Muslim soldiers, you would surrender; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said that there were nine soldiers in your group in total, including yourself. Today, you've mentioned that there were ten people. Can I confirm, which is correct, were there nine members or were there ten members of your group?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, again, when you gave your statement in the year 2000 and 2001, you couldn't recall clearly how many people were with you, and again this is an indication that your recollection of events was not so clear?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your statement, you go on to describe how a truck came along and that your group surrendered to local Muslims. You said that those people treated you in a fair manner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You then go on to explain that you were taken to a school or a local community centre, where you were detained for two or three hours, and then taken by truck to a Mujahedin camp. Do you have any idea approximately what time of day it was when you surrendered? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: It was in the morning. When we came across those three soldiers on that road, about 10.00, 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then you spent some time at this local school or community centre, and then you were transported to the Mujahedin camp. Could it have been afternoon or even evening by the time you arrived at the Mujahedin camp?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: It was still daytime, afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, concerning the total length of time that you spent in the Mujahedin camp, in your statement you say the following: "I am not able to tell how many days we spent at this camp. Most probably seven to ten days." Again, is this an indication that you didn't have a clear recollection of the events that took place at the camp?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Not only did I not have a clear recollection, I wanted no recollection at all. As for the other persons who were there with me, we're not in touch at all so we never talk about it, not even when we just happened to bump into each other like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: As for the dates, the truth about that, I said what I said without having prepared myself, having thought it over, just like I'm telling you today. I hadn't prepared in order to tell the exact dates, the exact minute, the exact facts. You can talk to the remaining ten people if you want to know about the dates, if you want to know about morning, afternoon, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay, I understand. It's a long time ago, and I understand that your recollection is not so good. But I appreciate you trying to answer the questions. At the time when you arrived at the camp, would you agree with me that combat activities were still going on in the Ozren-Vozuca area and further north in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And during the time that you were in the camp, would you accept that there was a lot of activity going on that you could see? For example, in the video that we saw today, we saw that there were a lot of men that appeared to be training, moving around, preparing for combat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: You obviously can't comprehend the situation that we found ourselves in. We weren't exactly walking around that camp. We were keeping our heads down, walking around with no shoes on, dirty shirts on, bleeding, hands and legs restrained, lying on the floor in that room, all covered in blood, our ribs broken. We were certainly no tourists in that place, if that's what you're thinking. We did emerge from that building a couple of times, but only keeping our heads down, and yet we could still notice that. Those were the observations that we had, and the same applies to all the other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll come to the times that you came out of the building in a moment, but if I could ask you about something else at this stage. According to your statement, you were taken to a house, where you were put in a room on the left-hand side, next to the entrance. If I can ask you about the building in which you were placed. You were shown some photographs today, and you said that you were 95 per cent certain that that was the building in which you were placed. Did the building in which you were placed have a roof, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the photographs we saw today, it looks similar, but you can't be certain, you can't be sure, that that was the place that you were put in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Were all members of your group, in other words, all ten men, placed into the same room in the building?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, apart from Mile Gojic, who after about two or three days converted to Islam, so he was put in some other room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the room in which you were placed, was that the room that we saw in the video clip, the room where you were all sitting around and you pointed out yourself and Mile Gojic as being people on the video clip?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. No, no, no. That's the room under that one, five by five, four by four, windows boarded up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, just to clarify, you were kept in a room underneath the room we saw on the video clip; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when you were in the room where you were detained, were all the nine men in your group in close proximity to each other? In other words, would you have all been able to see and hear the same things that were taking place within the room?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Ten, ten, not nine. Ten, and then in addition to those, another three or four for a day or two from the Ozren unit, and we could all hear it, we could all see what was going on, notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that there were already four Serb prisoners in the room when you arrived. Now you've just mentioned that there were three or four others. Could you be mistaken about there being other men in the room when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I don't think I could, it's not possible, but -- it's not realistic to expect me to remember every single thing. I don't think it's even respectful, in a way. Again, there are ten other people out there for you. Cross-reference their statements, use them to establish the facts. You can get an investigator to do that for you, and I'm certain that you'll easily arrived at what you're after.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that you may find this difficult, but I can assure you that your testimony is very important, and I'm trying not to make you uncomfortable in putting these questions to you. I'd like to turn to the part of the statement where you talk about the person in the room who was next to you. You said that you spoke to that person. In your statement, you didn't mention the name of that man. Am I correct in saying that you didn't find out his name?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is that because you only spoke to that man for a very short period of time?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: A couple of sentences, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you've told us today that there were three or four people in the room when you arrived. Am I correct in saying that you didn't find out the names of the other two or three men in that room when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I didn't find the name out, the first or the last name, and there was no time for that, either. I would like to clarify that a bit for you. These were members of this Ozren unit which was a casualty in that camp. The next day, because of all of that, they were moved to another room next to ours. After that we didn't have any contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that the next day they were taken out of your room sometime before noon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: During your period of detention at the camp, in your statement you describe how you were taken by jeep back to the Vozuca area to collect a heavy machine-gun. Do you remember describing that?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you remember when you paid that visit to the Vozuca area? Was it the same day that you arrived or was it on a later stage during your detention?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So this was one of the occasions when you were taken outside of the building and you could see something of the camp; am I right?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were occasions when you were allowed outside the building. Is it correct that you were allowed outside on two other occasions during your period of detention? One other occasion was when you and the other men were tasked with picking up rubbish around the camp; is that so?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And on another occasion, you were all allowed out of the room to wash yourself with soap and cold water?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, before the filming. It was on the upper floor, because we were all stinking of urine and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So during those different occasions when you were outside of the building, you did have an opportunity to see something of the camp?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you notice whether there were any horses around the camp?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you see any Serb prisoners of war looking after any horses? It obviously follows that you didn't, from your last answer, but am I right?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: No, those who were captured, those four from the Ozren unit, one of them was somebody who took care of horses, and in the hills or mountains the military transport is always using horses. I assume that they were separated from the Ozren groups because they were horse-handlers. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness -- sorry, sir. Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Try to get closer to the microphone. The interpreters don't hear you very well when you're sitting very far from the microphone. And try to speak a little louder. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And during the period of your detention, would you agree with me that at no time did you see any Serb prisoners of war cooking or preparing food for either your group or Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: No, I didn't, I definitely didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about what you said in your statement about what this man told you, the man next to you, when you arrived in the room. You have told us that you have difficulties recollecting the events. You've told us that you only spoke to this man for a couple of sentences. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- you describe how the man next to you said that he and the other men with him had been caught in the Vozuca area and that the Arabs were taking people out of the house to be executed. According to your statement, the man said that they were cooks or horsemen so that was the reason why they were saved up 'til that moment. Can you explain for us what you meant in the statement? You've told us that there weren't any horses at the Mujahedin camp, and you've told us that these men were not being used to cook food for anybody else. Is there any explanation?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Of course, I don't know how you are connecting the horses with these instances of people having their hands and feet bound by wire. When we came, there were four. Upstairs, there were people who were still alive. I think he said ten, seven or ten, something like that. I saw about 10 to 15 people upstairs on the first floor at that time when we were being interrogated. My question was, "What are our chances of surviving," to which he told me to keep quiet and said that they were bringing people out, killing them, massacring them. So obviously those four were eyewitnesses of those events. One of them was totally crazy. He had gone mad. He was talking to himself. People were stressed out, just like we were, of course. But these four were completely out of their mind. The next day, they were taken off to a separate room, and the last time we saw them was when they brought out that old man who died in the room where we were. And then two or three days later, we heard how they were being hit, beaten, and that's how we could tell they were still alive. Well, I assume what their fate was if they were eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. So just in relation to the person that you spoke to, you've told us that the four in the room were out of their mind. This man was talking about horses and he was talking about being cooked. Am I right in saying that this man was not talking any sense?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: It did make sense. You are not correct. They were just in that state. The one who was sitting next to me, he was still relatively normal, although he was under stress and very disturbed and upset. He was telling me to keep quiet, and a couple of minutes later that he kept telling me to be quiet, not to say anything, not to ask anything, that we weren't allowed to talk, after a couple of minutes, five or six of those Mujahedin came in again, and then the kicking started and so on and so forth. I don't want to bother you with all of that and take up your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were some prisoners upstairs. In your statement you don't say how many persons you saw. Today, you've mentioned a figure, 10 to 15. Could you explain? Why did you not mention the figure of 10 to 15 when you gave your statement? Could you be -- could you be mistaken when you mention those figures?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figures. I saw those people up there for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that at no time were you able to ascertain the identities of those people?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Their identity was told to me by that person that I sat next to in the room downstairs, that those were members of the Ozren unit that had been captured at Vozuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You didn't find out any names of those people, though?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Which ones, the ones upstairs or the ones downstairs? The ones upstairs, of course I couldn't find out their names. At the time when I was being taken upstairs for interrogation, I noticed, just in passing in a couple of seconds, 10 or 15 people sitting down, with their hands behind their backs and their heads bowed between their knees, sitting on the floor. At that point in time, I was given a blow, a kick to my stomach, and I fell and so on and so forth. My hands were tied behind my back. I was barefoot, so I couldn't really pay attention and count how many there were. I couldn't even raise my head, never mind anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. This would be an appropriate moment to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like to turn to the part in your statement where you describe the second day of detention, and you say that a certain time in the day, you heard noises coming from the stairs. Later on, you heard the noise of what sounded like pistol shots. As I understand your statement, you only heard noises and you could not see what was happening outside your room. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It follows that you could not tell who was moving around outside, and you couldn't tell how many people were out there, could you?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Perhaps I would need to clarify that a little bit for you. This happened on the second or the third day. I don't know exactly which day. I don't know the exact time, either. I know it was daytime. Suddenly, you could hear shouts and a stampede down the stairs leading to the first floor, and there were shouts and cries in a foreign language, in Arabic. I assume that the stampede was people quickly coming down these stairs, and then after --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Witness, I appreciate that you wish to tell your story, but if perhaps I could just explain to you your statement of evidence has already been admitted into evidence, which explains your account of what you saw and what you heard.

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has read that, so are aware of your account. I am seeking to clarify certain aspects of your account today, so I'd be very grateful if you could please focus on the questions that I'm putting to you. But staying on this topic, what I would like to put to you is part of a statement given by another person who was detained with you. I will not reveal the name of that person to you, but what this person said is: "While walking freely in the camp, I could not see the Mujahedin having military training, but I could hear that they had an area where they went to train, shooting." Now, that person has said in a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that he could hear that there was an area that the Mujahedin went to train at shooting. You have told us that you went outside of the building on several occasions. Do you accept that there was an area where the Mujahedin went to train at shooting?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it would follow from that that it was not -- that it was normal or there was nothing special to hear shooting from time to time while you were detained at the camp?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: You couldn't hear it every day, and then from this you could derive -- if I may come out with an assumption of my own, after five to ten minutes, and this is was systematic. After five to ten minutes, I assumed that people were being taken for execution. You could hear bullets from a pistol. After each shot, 10 or 15 seconds, you would hear pistol shots, because a rifle, a pistol, an automatic rifle, make different sounds. So after each shooting, 10 or 15 seconds later -- I mean, I don't know if somebody would be practicing shooting from a pistol, but they wouldn't wait 10 or 15 seconds between each individual firing, between each shot. So this would be my assumption, because after that nothing would be heard more from these people. And to tell you the truth, there was also some sort of yellow loader there, so it was my assumption, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've been fair by saying --

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: -- allow me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm correct in saying that you did not hear any shouts, or cries, or anything like that, did you, at the time that you heard these shots outside?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: The shooting was some 50 to 100 metres away. I didn't hear any cries. I heard the cries at the point in time when those 10 or 15 people would start from upstairs. I would hear the shouting in Arabic, the fast descent down the stairs, the stampede.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. I want to move to a different topic now. In your statement, you mention that you received food and water whilst you were in detention. Am I correct in saying that water was provided to you in plastic containers, oil bottles, or whatever was available to hold water, different types of things?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: On the second day, it was in a tin pail or bucket, and only on the third day we received a bowl of rice and one head of cabbage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So in your statement you say that "During the second night, an old man was brought into our room. His name was probably Nenad Jovic." Can you explain why you say his name was "probably Nenad Jovic"? Did he not tell you his name?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: In those kinds of moments, you cannot really remember somebody's first and last name, but I'm sure that his name was not Jovic but Galic. Either his first name was Nenad or his last name was Galic, and he was an elderly man, in age from 70 to 80 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You said that he drank water mixed with oil and got ill. Was this the tin pail or the bucket that you'd mentioned a moment ago that he drank from?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the Mujahedin would give you whatever they had available to hold water, and that this bucket or pail had been used to carry oil or diesel at some earlier stage; in other words, it just had traces of oil on it?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, traces of oil. I also drank from there, and nothing happened to me. The others also drank from it. But what happened to him, to Jovic -- not Jovic but this Galic, either Nenad Galic or -- either his first name was Nenad or his last name was Galic. He was an old man of 70 to 80 years old. They were looking for his son, who was in Doboj. And they took him out -- I would just like to clarify more how he died. He was an elderly man, 70 to 80 years old. He didn't know where he was, actually. And they didn't tie his feet or his hands. He was banging on the door, asking them to let him out because he needed to go and feed the cattle, and at that point a Mujahedin came in, knocked him down, and hit him two or three times on the back and on his backside. He hit him with a black baton, but they were not blows that could cause his death. But, I mean, I don't know, he was an elderly man, so I don't know what could have happened. All I know is that the next day, he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And I know you're not a medical specialist, but you would agree that it's not possible to ascertain how this old man died?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, earlier on today you were shown some photographs, stills taken from the video clip, where there was you and the other members of your group in the room, and we saw Mile Gojic wearing a yellow jacket. Can you tell us how long you had been detained at the camp, approximately, when that video was taken? Was it towards the end of your stay there?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: This was three days -- three, four days -- two, three, four days before the military police came and before we were taken to the Zenica prison, this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then if I can move towards concluding my questions. In all the time that you were detained in the camp, and you've described what happened to the old man, you never actually saw anyone being killed, did you?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Well [as interpreted], I just have to add something because of the Trial Chamber. I just remembered this. When we came to the camp on the first day, one of the four that were already in that room not only told me that they were bringing people out, killing them and massacring them, but that there were seven of them were left upstairs, and that's what I put together with that other thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could just correct a matter of the record. On page 36, at line 12, the witness initially answered: "Correct," and it's been recorded as "well."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Witness, can you just confirm that when I asked you the question, your initial answer was, "Correct," and then you went on to explain about the four other persons?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm sorry, you have to explain a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have to put the question again to him and ask him to answer it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll put the question to you once again, Witness. In all the time that you were detained in the camp, you never actually saw anyone being killed, did you?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us how on several occasions you went outside of the building, and we know that eventually you left the camp and were taken to Zenica. In all the times that you went outside, you didn't see any signs that people had been killed at the camp, did you?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't see any, other than the things that I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the people -- the noises that you heard outside, the other people that you have told us about that were in the building, you cannot exclude the possibility that those people were taken away from the camp during the course of your detention there?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I'm convinced that they were executed there, and this is why, if I can explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, you've answered my question. And, Your Honours, that was my final question, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be allowed to explain the basis for which he is convinced that the persons were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you if you could please explain how you came to that conclusion or how you became convinced that these people were executed there, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: I already said that, because of the shooting, but number 1, the first contact on the first day with those four, one of those four told me that they were killing, cutting throats, massacring, that they were eyewitnesses, that people were crazed from having seen that. And next to that, the other fact is that when this elderly man died, they brought a wheelbarrow and we put him in the wheelbarrow, stiff as he was, and we thought that they would allow us to bury him somewhere. After that, we were brought back to that room, and they brought out those four who were in the other room, and they then probably took that old man in the wheelbarrow to bury him. I assume so. I assume that they didn't want to allow us, because they decided that we were to be exchanged and because they decided to keep us alive or to let us live, I assume that they did not want to show us the place where the people who were killed were actually buried, where the place of burial was. I don't know if you understood me. Maybe I can explain some more. Those four who had already witnessed the executions before, they took that old man to the place where people were being buried. We were not allowed -- the group of ten of us were not permitted to do that so that the next day we wouldn't be able to point out this gravesite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, PW-12. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, I just have one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The gentleman who was sitting next to you, one of the four that you found in the room when you arrived, who you thought -- or who you told us, you said, they were cooks or horsemen, did they tell you where they were cooking or keeping horses?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: That area, it's a hilly area. Horses were used to transport items and kitchen items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Used by who?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: The army. It was a mountainous area with an elevation of over 1.000 metres, so transport of items and kitchen items was done with horses. These were just paths. There were no roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which army was using horses?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: All of them had to use horses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my original question was: Where did they do this cooking or keep the horses? Can you just answer that part, that question? Not even where. My question was: Did he tell you where they cooked and where they kept horses?

utterances.speaker: PW-12
utterances.text: No, no, he didn't tell me anything like that. There was no time for a conversation like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to find out. Any questions arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, thank you very much. This brings us to the end of your testimony here. May I take the time to say thank you very much for coming to testify. You are now excused, you may stand down, and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, may we lift the curtain, please, or the blind. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as previously indicated to the Defence and to the Chamber's legal officer, the next witness is not available to testify until tomorrow, so we have no further witnesses for today. We have one witness tomorrow and then one witness on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that's the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For now, there is a possibility perhaps of a witness for Monday, the 10th, but we have nothing further for today. We have just the remaining two witnesses scheduled for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned, and we'll come back tomorrow at 9.00 in the same courtroom, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 11.10 a.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
